power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Agreement attraction in comprehension often manifests itself as a speed-up in the of processing ungrammatical sentences where a verb carries the wrong number feature when a noun of the verb-matching number-the attractor-intervenes.
The effect has been claimed to be insensitive to increased linear distance between the attractor and the agreement target.
Recent studies on Czech found weak attraction effects attested only with case syncretic attractors.

In two self-paced reading experiments with Czech comprehenders, we tested whether including material between the attractor and the verb could modulate attraction depending on whether the material was reinforcing the attractor's features or not.
In Experiment 1, we aimed to increase attraction strength by modifying the attractor with a relative clause, giving it the subject feature and reinforcing its plurality.
In Experiment 2, we matched the increased distance employed in Experiment 1 with feature-inert material to see if attraction was maintained.
Our Bayes factor analysis provided us with evidence of a small attraction effect in the both experiments that did not differ meaningfully between the two.
We therefore show that Czech exhibits online number attraction but of a tiny effect size.

Our results further replicate earlier findings that distance does not affect agreement attraction in comprehension, as our effect sizes were comparable between the two experiments as well with previous work on Czech.
Finally, they show that modifying attractors with relative clauses does not increase the strength of attraction speed-ups.
Agreement attraction speech errors such as the following often occur in production (Bock & Miller, 1991; Bock & Cutting, 1992): (1) *The editor of the history books were competent.
text.formatted: Agreement attraction speech errors such as the following often occur in production <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bock & Miller, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bock & Cutting, 1992)</ref>: (1) *The editor of the history books were competent.

text.text: Sentence (1) is ungrammatical, since the verb were ought to be the was due to the agreement controller subject head the editor being singular.

Speakers are more likely to produce a number agreement error in using a plural-marked verb when there is a plural distractor noun (known as the attractor), in this case intervening between the subject head and the verb compared to cases where the noun is singular (Bock & Miller, 1991; Bock et al., 2001; Vigliocco et al., 1995; Hartsuiker et al., 2003).

text.text: Moreover, agreement attraction occurs in comprehension as well. Wagers et al. (2009) exposed their English speaking participants to ungrammatical sentences such as (1) and observed that their RTs were sped-up when the attractor (e.g., books) was plural compared to when it was singular.

text.text: Comprehenders also often come under the illusion that attraction sentences such as (1) are grammatical even though they are not (Wagers et al., 2009; Hammerly et al., 2019; Royer, 2021).

text.text: Agreement attraction in comprehension has been replicated both in English (Tanner et al., 2014; Parker & An, 2018; Cunnings & Sturt, 2018) and in a myriad of other languages (Lago et al., 2015; Lago & Felser, 2018; Lago et al., 2021; Avetisyan et al., 2020; Tucker et al., 2015 Tucker et al., , 2021;; Franck et al., 2015; Franck & Wagers, 2020; Bhatia & Dillon, 2022; Slioussar, 2018; Bleotu & Dillon, 2022; Ivanova-Sullivan et al., 2024; Sturt & Kwon, 2024; Türk & Logačev, 2024), making it arguably one of the most thoroughly cross-linguistically validated effect in language processing. Jäger et al. (2020) conducted a large controlled replication and found that attraction can be reliably observed in English, while a Bayesian meta-analysis estimated the size of the effect to be centred at -22 ms (Jäger et al., 2017).

(2015), who see the effect as arising via domain-general mechanisms within the cue-based retrieval approach (Parker et al., 2017; Lewis & Vasishth, 2005; Engelmann et al., 2019).

(2015)</ref>, who see the effect as arising via domain-general mechanisms within the cue-based retrieval approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Parker et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Lewis & Vasishth, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Engelmann et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the phenomenon has received many theoretical explanations next to cue-based retrieval, such as feature percolation accounts (e.g., Eberhard et al., 2005), self-organising sentence processing (Smith et al., 2018), and a recent theory based on the SOB-Complex span working memory model (Keshev et al., 2025).

text.text: However, recent studies on one language have shown the limits of the universality of the effect.

Chromý, Lacina and colleagues (Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil, 2023; Chromý, Brand, et al., 2023; Chromý et al., 2025; Lacina & Chromý, 2022; Lacina & Dotlačil, 2024; Lacina et al., 2025) conducted a series of attraction studies on Czech comprehension (and in one experiment on Slovak).

text.text: Overall, they found very little evidence for the presence of the effect.
Most of the experiments, analysed with Bayesian models, showed evidence in favour of no attraction effects either in number or gender agreement.
In their research, attraction effects surfaced only under case syncretism.
This is when a single word form corresponds to more than one combination of features such as number, gender or case (Caha, 2019).
text.formatted: This is when a single word form corresponds to more than one combination of features such as number, gender or case <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Caha, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Only when the attractor noun had the same form as the nominative was a very small attraction effect seen in reading (-12ms in Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil, 2023) and in grammaticality illusions (4% increase in acceptability in Lacina & Dotlačil, 2024).

text.text: Similar results regarding the crucial role of case syncretism in Slavic attraction were reported by Badecker & Kuminiak (2007) and Slioussar (2018) foot_0 .

text.text: However, even under the case syncretism, the effect of agreement attraction was extremely weak and hard to detect: Bayes factor analysis showed no evidence against attraction but it also showed no clear evidence for attraction, even under very narrow priors.
Nonetheless, it appears that if there is any attraction in Czech, it only occurs when there is confusion as to what the subject is.
This could be accommodated within the retrieval-as-repair strategy as originally proposed by Wagers et al. (2009).
text.formatted: This could be accommodated within the retrieval-as-repair strategy as originally proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Wagers et al. (2009)</ref>.

text.text: The idea is that retrieval processes only kick in when an anomaly is detected.

If confusion about subjecthood is the key to attraction effects in the language, it is plausible that should the attractor appear even more like a possible subject of the matrix clause, attraction effects would increase in strength.
This is the empirical question of the current study.
Within standard retrospective attraction set-ups, the attractor is placed as an unmodified noun within the NP that contains the subject head.
We hypothesise that modifying the attractor noun with a subject relative clause (RC) strengthens the attraction speed-up.
The reason for this is that the attractor could be represented as the subject of its RC, appearing even more subject-like.
Additionally, Czech relative pronouns as well as verbs within relative clauses also exhibit number agreement.
This means that when a particular noun is relativised on, its number feature is repeated with agreement markers several times in the course of processing.
When encountered by comprehenders, this could additionally reinforce the plurality of attractors in memory.

Using RC modification introduces the subject feature to the attractor, reinforces the plurality of the attractor yet also simultaneously increases the distance between the attractor noun and the verb.
The results of Parker & Phillips (2016) suggested that distance alone does not turn off attraction effects in English.

text.text: They contrasted two potentially attraction-inducing structures: (2) *According to the janitor, the key to the cabinets probably were destroyed by the fire.
(3) *The key to the cabinets, according to the janitor, probably were destroyed by the fire.
In (3), the parenthetical intervenes between the attractor and the verb, whereas in (2), it precedes the subject and the attractor. Parker & Phillips (2016) found attraction with both (2) and (3).
text.formatted: In (3), the parenthetical intervenes between the attractor and the verb, whereas in (2), it precedes the subject and the attractor. <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Parker & Phillips (2016)</ref> found attraction with both (2) and (3).

text.text: However, it remains unclear whether Czech comprehenders, who show very weak effects already, would also prove invulnerable to increased distance.

Taking this together then, we believe there is a reason to test whether in Czech, attraction effects can be either strengthened or weakened by the inclusion of further material between the attractor and the verb.
We predict that including material reinforcing the number and subject features of the attractor would strengthen the effect.
According to earlier results on English, simply increasing the distance with feature-irrelevant material should not diminish the effect.
We ran two web-based self-paced reading experiments with large samples of native speakers of Czech.
In Experiment 1, we tested whether by making the attractor the subject of its RC, we could strengthen the previously identified small attraction effect.
In Experiment 2, we included feature-inert material (a series of of adverbs) and asked if it could diminish or turn off the effect.
All of our anonymised data as well as the analysis scripts are available here: OSF project repository.
We implemented a 2 × 2 factorial within-subject within-item design in both experiments.
We manipulated verb and attractor number within our items.
As our starting point, we took the items from Experiment 4 reported in Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil (2023).
text.formatted: As our starting point, we took the items from Experiment 4 reported in <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil (2023)</ref>.

text.text: These sentences consisted of a subject NP, which included the subject head in the singular, the preposition pro ('for'), the attractor noun, which was either in the singular or the plural depending on the condition, an adverb, the future tense auxiliary either in the singular or plural, again dependent on the condition, an infinitive verb followed by the rest of the sentence, whose structure was varied.
What we added to these items was a relative clause modifying the attractor noun that was placed between the attractor and the adverb preceding the auxiliary.
The relative clause included the word která/které ('which.SG'/'which.PL'), which varied according to the number of the attractor.
This was followed by an adverb and a verb in the present tense, which was conjugated according to the number of the attractor.
See an example item below: Experiment 2 replaced the added RC with a series of adverbs.
This was done in order to replicate the same distance (measured in words) that was created in Experiment 1 by means of inserting the RC.
Adverbs were used due to them not containing any features relevant for agreement such as number or gender.
See an example below: Altogether, there were 32 critical items and 64 filler items.
Each sentence was followed by a yes-no comprehension question that was targeting pieces of information within it.
For Experiment 1, 322 participants were recruited from the pool of students at Charles University, Prague, who received course credit.
We excluded 19 non-native Czech speakers and nine participants who self-reported dyslexia.

The average age was 22 years (sd = 3.8). 19 participants were removed because they self-identified as non-native speakers, another 9 participants were removed because they self-identified as dyslexics, and 14 participants were removed because their reading time fell below 100 ms per word for at least 10% of the words and/or they had more than 20% of mistakes in their answers to comprehension questions.
The median of correct answers to the comprehension questions was 95% (before the exclusion).
Experiment 2 saw 209 participants from the same pool.
The average age was 23 years (sd = 4.5).
We excluded 8 self-identified non-native speakers and 7 self-identified dyslexics. 15 participants were removed using the same exclusion criteria as in Experiment 1.
The median of correct answers to the comprehension questions was 94% (before the exclusion).
The experiments, distributed via a link, were hosted on PCIbex (Zehr & Schwarz, 2018) and employed the moving window word-by-word self-paced reading paradigm.
text.formatted: The experiments, distributed via a link, were hosted on PCIbex <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Zehr & Schwarz, 2018)</ref> and employed the moving window word-by-word self-paced reading paradigm.

text.text: The participants first read a consent form and filled in their demographic and linguistic background.
Next, they were exposed to several practice sentences.
Each item was followed by a comprehension question that was to be answered by clicking on 'yes' or 'no'.
There was no feedback or a time-out.
The items were distributed based on the Latin Square design.
Each participant was exposed to eight instances of each condition.
We ran Bayesian hierarchical models with log-normal likelihood predicting reading times in the critical post-verbal region.
We used the package brms (Bürkner, 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2026).
text.formatted: We used the package brms <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bürkner, 2017)</ref> in R (R Core Team, 2026).

text.text: The model included verb number (i.e. grammaticality), attractor number, and their interaction as fixed effects.
We included the full random effects structure containing both intercepts and slopes for the two main effects and their interaction.

We used regularising priors, which were set in the following way: • Intercept: Normal(6,1) • Fixed effects: Normal(0,0.5) • Random effects: Normal+(0,0.5) (half-normal truncated at 0), with LKJ distribution η = 2 for correlation matrices (Lewandowski et al., 2009) • Residual standard deviation: Normal+(0, 1) (half-normal truncated at 0).

text.text: We ran 3,000 iterations using 4 chains with the first half of samples discarded as warm-up.
All R values were below 1.02, indicating convergence.

We also ran a Bayes factor analysis to quantify evidence for the full model, including the interaction term as a fixed effect, compared to the almost identical model, which only lacks the interaction term as a fixed effect.
The model was run for 20,000 samples, 2,000 warm-up, Bayes factor was calculated using the Savage-Dickey ratio method (see Schad et al. (2023) for introduction).
text.formatted: The model was run for 20,000 samples, 2,000 warm-up, Bayes factor was calculated using the Savage-Dickey ratio method (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Schad et al. (2023)</ref> for introduction).

text.text: We selected two priors for the Bayes Factor analysis: Normal(-0.027, 0.009) and Normal(-0.0135, 0.0045).
We use negative priors since facilitatory interference of the attractor in ungrammatical sentences, vs. the lack thereof in grammatical sentences, should show as a negative interaction.
The values are based on the estimates of the agreement attraction effects provided in the metaanalysis of attraction experiments in Jäger et al. (2017); Schad et al. (2023).

text.text: These priors, with means rounded to the second decimal point, were also used by Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil (2023) in their Bayes factor analysis.

text.text: In that work, none of their four experiments revealed clear evidence in favour of the model with the interaction term with these priors.

There, the results generally favoured the model without the interaction term, and only in the experiment with syncretic forms was there anecdotal evidence, with BF10 above 1 but smaller than 3, for the interaction term model).

text.text: We focus on the post-verb region in our discussion.
This region shows a substantial ungrammaticality effect, manifested as a slow-down in the conditions with the plural auxiliary.
As for the main effect of the number of the attractor, the 95% Credible Intervals included zero.
Most importantly for us, the 95% Credible Intervals of the posterior estimate for the interaction term did not include zero (estimate=-0.008, 95% CrI: [-0.014, -0.002]).
We now turn to the Bayes factor analysis.
For the prior Normal(-0.027, 0.009), the Bayes factor BF10 , measuring the evidence in favour of the model with the interaction, was 1.5.
For the prior Normal(-0.0135, 0.0045), we saw BF10 of 13.0.
Recall that values lower than 1 indicate evidence in favour of the model without the interaction, values higher than 1 indicate evidence in favour of the model with the interaction.

Values in the range 1/3-1/10 are sometimes labelled as moderate evidence for the null model, values in the range of 3-10 are sometimes labelled as moderate evidence    for the alternative model (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014) and values higher than 10/lower than 1/10 are labelled as strong evidence for the alternative or the null model, respectively.

text.text: In sum, there is borderline moderate-to-strong evidence for the model with the interaction term, but only in case of a very restricted prior.

This supports the summary of the posterior distributions, which shows that the 95% credible interval of the interaction term, while excluding zero, does not range lower than -0.014, albeit with the caveat that the posterior values of the interaction term are closer to zero in Czech than in most other languages (see also Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil (2023)).

text.text: In the post-verb region we see a clear ungrammaticality effect, manifested as a slow-down in the conditions with the plural auxiliary.
Just as in Experiment 1, we also see an effect of interaction.
The 95% Credible Intervals of the posterior estimate for the interaction term is on the borderline of including zero (estimate=-0.006, 95% CrI: [-0.013, 0.000]).
We now turn to the Bayes factor analysis.
For the prior Normal(-0.027, 0.009), the Bayes factor BF10 , measuring the evidence in favour of the model with the interaction, was 0.2.
For the prior Normal(-0.0135, 0.0045), we saw the BF10 as 1.6.
That is, we see that the prior assuming a larger effect shows borderline moderate evidence in favour of the model without the interaction term.
For a narrower prior, the evidence switches in favour of the model with the interaction but since the value stays below 3, it is indecisive.
In Experiment 1, the BF10 value for the narrow prior was slightly above 10, providing moderate-to-strong evidence for the model with the interaction term.
In order to evaluate whether the strength of the attraction effect observed in Experiments 1 and 2 differs, we conducted a joint analysis of both datasets.

The model had the same structure but included an extra fixed effect, Experiment (contrast-coded such that the second experiment is coded as +1, the first experiment as -1), and the interaction of Experiment with Verb Number, with Attractor Number, and the three-way interaction.
The model included the maximal random structure for subjects and items random effects.
The prior and sampling were the same as in Experiment 1 and 2.
The posterior distributions are summarised in Figure 5.
text.formatted: The posterior distributions are summarised in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref>.

text.text: We see a clear negative effect of the verb number × attractor number interaction, i.e., the signal of agreement attraction (estimate=-0.007, 95% CrI: [-0.012, -0.0021]).
At the same time, there is no interaction of agreement attraction with the experiment (verb number × attractor number × experiment, estimate=-0.0002, 95% CrI: [-0.005, 0.004]).
Finally, to investigate the size of evidence for the verb number × attractor number interaction in the joint dataset, we computed a Bayes factor analysis.
The models were identical to the ones used for Experiment 1 and 2, but they have one additional factor, experiment.
The models reveal evidence for agreement attraction in the joint dataset: For the prior Normal(-0.027, 0.009), we saw BF10 of 5.5.
For the prior Normal(-0.0135, 0.0045), we saw BF10 of 45.8.

In sum, the joint dataset provides moderate evidence for a slightly broad prior, and strong evidence for agreement attraction when the prior is kept narrow, i.e., narrower than what one would expect based on the previous research on agreement attraction.
Does making attractors more subject-like by modifying them with relative clauses (RCs) increase the strength of facilitatory speed-ups in attraction configurations?

In our Experiments 1 and 2, we attempted to expand the research on agreement attraction in comprehension by conducting a selfpaced reading study with native speakers of Czech in which we tested whether number attraction effect size could be modulated by (a) RC modification and (b) simple distance.
In Experiment 1, we modified the attractor with a subject RC.
This achieved two effects, it increased the distance between the attractor and the verb and crucially, it gave the attractor the feature of being the subject of the RC.

We hypothesised that assigning the attractor an additional feature that would make it appear more subject-like, i.e., being made the subject of an RC, would strengthen the agreement attraction speed-up in ungrammatical sentences in cases of mismatching number between the verbal auxiliary and the (matrix-)subject head.
This was based on the idea first advocated by Wagers et al. (2009), who put forward that attraction only occurs when there is sufficient confusion as to what the subject is.
text.formatted: This was based on the idea first advocated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Wagers et al. (2009)</ref>, who put forward that attraction only occurs when there is sufficient confusion as to what the subject is.

text.text: In a recent study on gender attraction in Czech and Slovak by Lacina et al. (2025), this was suggested as one of the ways to explain the general lack of effects and their surfacing only under the condition of case syncretism with the nominative, that is when the attractor had the form that the subject takes in the language.
text.formatted: In a recent study on gender attraction in Czech and Slovak by <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Lacina et al. (2025)</ref>, this was suggested as one of the ways to explain the general lack of effects and their surfacing only under the condition of case syncretism with the nominative, that is when the attractor had the form that the subject takes in the language.

text.text: In Experiment 2, we replaced this additional intervening relative clause with feature-inert adverbial material of the same length measured in words to test whether (a) distance diminishes or turns off the effect and (b) any potential boosting effect of the relative clause in Experiment 1 was in fact masked by the contravening diminishing effect of increased distance.
In Experiment 1 (RCs), our Bayesian analysis showed a speed-up in reading times in the post-verbal region.
What this means is that in Experiment 1, number agreement attraction in ungrammatical sentences exhibited as facilitatory interference was present.
The Bayes factor analysis showed that we had evidence only in favour of a small effect rather than the effect size standardly reported in the literature (Jäger et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The Bayes factor analysis showed that we had evidence only in favour of a small effect rather than the effect size standardly reported in the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Jäger et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Experiment 2, on the other hand, did not provide the same evidence in favour of attraction with even the narrow prior not allowing us to draw any strong conclusions.
However, when we combine the two datasets, we see clearly that there is evidence for attraction, strong for a small effect and moderate even for the standardly sized effect.
The size of the effect does not meaningfully differ between the two experiments based on the joint analysis results.
In sum, we see that Czech shows number agreement attraction effects in reading but that the effect is substantially smaller compared to other languages studied.

The current research, therefore, joins the acceptability judgement results of Lacina & Dotlačil (2024), which reported tiny rates of grammaticality illusions in Czech with the same sentences with case-syncretic attractors that we used here, albeit additionally modified with RCs or distance.
text.formatted: The current research, therefore, joins the acceptability judgement results of <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Lacina & Dotlačil (2024)</ref>, which reported tiny rates of grammaticality illusions in Czech with the same sentences with case-syncretic attractors that we used here, albeit additionally modified with RCs or distance.

text.text: When we compare our results with the other study that used the current stimuli, Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil (2023), we see that adding the RC or increasing the distance does not meaningfully strengthen the effect.
text.formatted: When we compare our results with the other study that used the current stimuli, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil (2023)</ref>, we see that adding the RC or increasing the distance does not meaningfully strengthen the effect.

text.text: These researchers found only anecdotal evidence in favour of attraction in the experiment using syncrectism.
We strengthen that evidence, but not the size of the effect.
Most likely due to our larger sample size, we can now have more credence in the attraction effect observed and in its likely size.

When we take all of this together, we find that in general, the attraction effect in Czech is essentially invariant between the three configurations, i.e. no increased distance, RCs or adverbs inserted-it appears to be not influenced at all by additional intervening material, be it feature-relevant or feature-inert.

Therefore, our hypothesis derived from the idea that increasing the degree to which the attractor could be misconstrued as the subject would increase the strength of the attraction effect turned out to be incompatible with the current data.
This could be taken as going against the retrievalas-repair approach (Wagers et al., 2009).
text.formatted: This could be taken as going against the retrievalas-repair approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Wagers et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: However, the data could still be compatible with it-it could be claimed that subject-confusion could function in a binary way, that is if it crosses a certain threshold, retrieval is initiated as a means of repairing the ungrammatical structure.
At this point, the fact that the attractor is modified by an RC making it its subject is no longer relevant, as it does not influence the plural feature.
The current results ought to be discussed in relation to those of Parker & Phillips (2016), which tested both number agreement attraction and NPI illusions in English.
text.formatted: The current results ought to be discussed in relation to those <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">of Parker & Phillips (2016)</ref>, which tested both number agreement attraction and NPI illusions in English.

text.text: As mentioned in section 1, they found that adding more material between the attractor and the agreeing verb had no effect on attraction, while it turned the NPI illusion effect off.
Our current results support the attraction invariance finding and, arguably, improve on the design of Parker & Phillips (2016).
text.formatted: Our current results support the attraction invariance finding and, arguably, improve on the design of <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Parker & Phillips (2016)</ref>.

text.text: In their study, they used parentheticals such as according to the janitor, which included a noun marked for number (janitor ), which could have played a role in the process of establishing agreement.
On the other hand, our Experiment 2 used feature-inert adverbs to increase the distance between the attractor and the verb.
The pattern of results, however, remains the same-the attraction effect surfaced, yet was no stronger or weaker compared to when this intervening adverbial material was not inserted.

What our study additionally contributes is the datum that there is no decrease or turning-off of the agreement attraction effect in reading times, since Parker & Phillips (2016) only used speeded judgements to target attraction.
text.formatted: What our study additionally contributes is the datum that there is no decrease or turning-off of the agreement attraction effect in reading times, since <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Parker & Phillips (2016)</ref> only used speeded judgements to target attraction.

text.text: This further supports the idea that number agreement attraction effects in comprehension are driven by retrieval interference, as increased distance can only lead to more memory decay for both the target of agreement as well as the attractor, but it cannot, being feature-inert in the current study, play the role of a further interference actor.
In the current study, we investigated the phenomenon of number agreement attraction in the comprehension of Czech sentences.

Based on previous research by Chromý, Brand, et al. (2023); Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil (2023); Lacina & Chromý (2022), we attempted to strengthen the facilitatory interference effect found in ungrammatical sentences by means of giving the attractor the subject feature in Experiment 1.

(2023)</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil (2023)</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Lacina & Chromý (2022)</ref>, we attempted to strengthen the facilitatory interference effect found in ungrammatical sentences by means of giving the attractor the subject feature in Experiment 1.

text.text: This was achieved by modifying the attractor with a subject relative clause.
In Experiment 2, we matched this introduced distance by replacing the relative clause with a series of adverbs.

What we found was that there was no difference in the strength of the attraction speed-up either between Experiment 1 and 2 or between our current data and those reported for Experiment 4 in Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil (2023), which used the same sentences without the added linguistic material intervening between the attractor and the verb.
text.formatted: What we found was that there was no difference in the strength of the attraction speed-up either between Experiment 1 and 2 or between our current data and those reported for Experiment 4 in <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chromý, Lacina, & Dotlačil (2023)</ref>, which used the same sentences without the added linguistic material intervening between the attractor and the verb.

text.text: Overall, our results are in line with the previous results of Parker & Phillips (2016), who found that attraction effects remain invariant under distance manipulations.
text.formatted: Overall, our results are in line with the previous results of <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Parker & Phillips (2016)</ref>, who found that attraction effects remain invariant under distance manipulations.

text.text: We expand on these findings by showing that the invariance is also observed in self-paced reading and does not depend on the additional material being a paranthetical.
Admittedly, our results do not provide any new theoretical insights into the attraction effect.
They do, however, provide additional empirical data and clarify the "Czech attraction anomaly".

Drawing on our current results and earlier studies, we can close with stating that number agreement attraction in Czech exists but that it is extremely small and only occurs when there is case syncretism.
